page: Amazon Web Services m4.16xlarge is a previous-generation general purpose instance built on the Xen hypervisor architecture. It features an Intel Xeon E5-2686 v4 processor operating at 2.3 GHz, delivering 64 virtual CPUs across 32 physical cores with hyper-threading enabled. The processor includes 45 MB of L3 cache alongside instruction sets such as AVX, AES, and FMA, though it lacks newer vector extensions like AVX-512 and AMX. The instance is provisioned with 256 GB of system memory, maintaining a balanced 1:4 vCPU-to-RAM ratio of 4 GB per vCPU.

The hardware configuration does not bundle local instance storage, requiring all persistent storage and root volumes to be provisioned via external network-attached services. For network throughput, the instance provides a baseline network bandwidth of 25 Gbps. Hardware acceleration is absent, with zero GPUs included in the configuration.

Benchmark results demonstrate a clear bifurcation between single-threaded and multi-threaded throughput. Single-core performance falls within the bottom 10 percent of evaluated instances, evidenced by a Geekbench single-core score of 907.0 and a stress-ng single-core score of 860.49. In contrast, parallel capabilities register in the middle 50 percent, achieving a multi-core Geekbench score of 8847.0, a PassMark CPU score of 34597.48, and multi-threaded bzip3 decompression at 52.79 GB/sec. Uncached memory read bandwidth reaches 96.26 GB/sec, while static web serving throughput measures 27.41 GB/sec.

Given its older architectural baseline and modest single-core throughput, the m4.16xlarge presents a tradeoff of high core density against lower per-thread execution speed. Resource density makes it suitable for horizontally distributed workloads, static web serving, fleet CI/CD compilation, enterprise background processing, and memory-backed caching layers like Redis that leverage its 256 GB memory footprint.
description: Amazon Web Services m4.16xlarge is a general purpose instance powered by an Intel Xeon E5-2686 v4 processor running at 2.3 GHz. Configured with 64 vCPUs across 32 physical cores and 256 GB of system RAM, it maintains a standard 1:4 vCPU-to-memory allocation. The system includes no local instance storage and no GPU accelerators, relying on network-attached storage while offering a 25 Gbps baseline network capability. Benchmark evaluations place its single-core compute within the lower decile of tested machines, while its aggregate multi-core metrics, memory bandwidth, and caching performance align with median general-purpose tiers. It achieves 38.41 million operations per second on Redis SET workloads and 27.41 GB per second in static web serving. Due to its balanced capacity and moderate per-core speed, it is best applied to distributed web fleets, batch processing, and caching tiers.
